36946: The debate in Mark 7 is about hand-washing and whether impurity on hands makes food impure, a Pharisaic tradition, not about pork. Scholars such as Daniel Boyarin and Matthew Thiessen read the comment as Jesus ruling that permitted food does not become defiled through unwashed hands. Others read the narrator's comment as Mark's application for a Gentile church. Jesus elsewhere sends a leper to the priest according to Moses.
36947: Many evangelical and mainstream scholars (for example R. T. France and Joel Marcus) still read the parenthesis as Mark's own conclusion that all foods are clean for Jesus' followers, in line with Acts 10 and Paul. They agree Jesus himself is presented as Torah-observant. The disagreement is real and scholarly: what did Jesus mean, and what did Mark mean for his readers?
36948: How we read this shapes whether Jesus is seen as against Judaism or as a Jewish teacher debating its practice, a key question for Jewish-Christian understanding.
36949: For suffering believers, Mark said that the cross was not the defeat of the Messiah but the shape of his kingship, and that fear and failure, like the disciples', could be met by a risen Lord who goes ahead of them.
36950: Mark challenges triumphant, power-centred Christianity. It invites readers to see God's reign in service, to admit their own blindness, and to keep following when the story feels unfinished.
36951: A carefully researched account, written for a patron, showing Jesus as the Saviour promised to Israel whose kingdom lifts the lowly and opens to the nations.
36952: Traditionally Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
36953: The writer was an educated Greek stylist who knew the Greek Old Testament intimately and wrote both this Gospel and Acts. He says he was not an eyewitness but investigated carefully. Paul's letters mention a Luke, 'the beloved physician', as a co-worker.
36954: Both volumes are dedicated to Theophilus and share style and themes. Irenaeus and the Muratorian fragment (late second century) name Luke. The 'we' passages in Acts suggest the author travelled with Paul, though some scholars treat them as a literary device or a source.
36955: Unknown; suggestions include Rome, Antioch, Achaia or Asia Minor
36956: Early prologues to the Gospel place Luke in Achaia, but this tradition is late and uncertain.
36957: 'Most excellent Theophilus', probably a well-to-do patron, and the wider Greek-speaking church
36958: Somewhere in the eastern Mediterranean or Rome
36959: Gentile and Jewish believers needed confidence that their faith was rooted in reliable history and in Israel's Scriptures, and that a movement led by a crucified Jew was neither a novelty nor a threat to public order.
36960: From the announcement to Zechariah in the days of Herod to the ascension near Bethany.
36961: Census under Quirinius in Judea sparks a tax revolt led by Judas the Galilean.
36962: Death of Augustus; Tiberius becomes emperor.
36963: John the Baptist begins preaching (Luke dates it to Tiberius' fifteenth year, c. 28-29).
36964: Jerusalem besieged and destroyed, events Luke's Jesus foretells with grief.
36966:
Luke begins with a formal preface like those of Greek historians and medical writers, announcing that he has investigated everything carefully and will write an orderly account so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught. Yet as soon as the story begins the style switches to sound like the Greek Old Testament: a childless priestly couple, an angel in the temple, songs that echo Hannah and the Psalms. Luke deliberately places Jesus inside Israel's sacred history and inside Roman world history at the same time.

He dates events by emperors and governors: the decree of Caesar Augustus, Quirinius governing Syria, the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Pontius Pilate. In Roman propaganda Augustus was the saviour who brought peace. Luke's angels announce to shepherds that the real Saviour, Messiah and Lord, has been born in David's town, and that heaven's peace rests on those God favours. The contrast would not be lost on Roman readers.

Luke's world was organised by patronage: wealthy benefactors gave gifts and expected honour and loyalty in return, and people invited to dinner those who could invite them back. Luke's Jesus repeatedly cuts across that system, telling hosts to invite the poor, the crippled and the blind who cannot repay, and telling his followers that whereas kings like to be called 'benefactors', among them the greatest must serve.
36968: Benefactors gave gifts and expected honour and returns. Luke's centurion is a patron who built a synagogue; Jesus tells disciples to lend expecting nothing and to host those who cannot repay, redirecting honour to God, the true benefactor.
36970: Luke begins and ends in the temple. Jesus' parents keep the purification law, offer the poor family's sacrifice of birds, and go up for Passover each year. The disciples are 'continually in the temple' after the ascension. Jesus' family is portrayed as devout and Torah-keeping.
36972: Samaritans and Jews shared descent from Israel and the Torah but disputed where God should be worshipped, with centuries of bitterness and violence. Making a Samaritan the hero who keeps the command to love one's neighbour was shocking.
36974: Who ate with whom marked status and belonging. Luke shows Jesus at many tables, with Pharisees, tax collectors and sinners, using meals to enact the kingdom's welcome.
36976: Simeon awaits 'the consolation of Israel', Anna speaks to all looking for 'the redemption of Jerusalem', and the Emmaus disciples had hoped Jesus would 'redeem Israel'. These were national hopes for liberation and restoration, which Luke affirms and reshapes.
36977:
Luke's opening chapters are among the most Jewish texts in the New Testament. Zechariah and Elizabeth are 'righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments'. Mary's song echoes Hannah's, praising a God who brings down the mighty and lifts the lowly and who has helped 'his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham'. Zechariah praises God for raising up a horn of salvation in David's house and remembering his holy covenant. The angel promises Mary that her son will have the throne of his father David and reign over the house of Jacob forever. A first-century Jew would hear all this as God at last keeping his covenant promises to Israel.

Jesus' first sermon in the Nazareth synagogue reads Isaiah 61, the Jubilee-like proclamation of good news to the poor and release for captives, and declares it fulfilled 'today'. The kingdom he proclaims is Israel's hope of God's reign arriving with justice for the poor, healing and forgiveness. Luke gives Pharisees a mixed and partly sympathetic role: Jesus dines with them, some warn him about Herod, and in Acts a Pharisee counsels tolerance. At the end the risen Jesus opens 'Moses and all the Prophets and the Psalms' to show that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that repentance and forgiveness would go out to all nations beginning from Jerusalem. For Luke, the inclusion of Gentiles is not a replacement of Israel but the light to the nations that Simeon saw, which is also 'glory to your people Israel'.
36979: Births of John and Jesus are told in the language of Israel's Scriptures, with songs of covenant fulfilment.
36981: John prepares the way; Jesus is anointed by the Spirit and announces Isaiah's year of the Lord's favour.
36983: Healings, calls, blessings and woes, and meals with sinners show the kingdom reversing status.
36984: On the long road Jesus teaches through parables about mercy, wealth, prayer and the lost being found.
36986: Jesus enters the city, mourns its coming fall, teaches in the temple and eats Passover with the twelve.
36988: Jesus is declared innocent by Pilate, forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a dying thief.
36990: The risen Jesus explains the Scriptures, breaks bread, commissions witnesses and ascends.
36991: Saviour for Israel and the nations
37014: Rescuer and rescue, titles also claimed for emperors; in Luke, God's deliverance of Israel and the world through Jesus.
37015: Marks salvation arriving in the present, not only the future.
37017: Release from debt or captivity, and forgiveness of sins; the Jubilee word in Isaiah 61.
37019: Divine necessity: God's purpose in Scripture had to be fulfilled.
37020: Volume two of the same work; the Gospel's ending overlaps the opening of Acts.
37021: Jesus' mission statement and Simeon's song draw on Isaiah's servant and Jubilee texts.
37022: Mary's song and the birth stories echo Hannah's song and Samuel's childhood.
37023: Jesus' family keeps the purification law, and the Nazareth sermon echoes the Jubilee.
37024: Luke uses Mark as one of the 'many' earlier accounts mentioned in his preface.
37025: Luke presents Jesus as Messiah, Lord and Saviour, the Spirit-anointed prophet like Moses, and the innocent righteous sufferer. Jewish readers often appreciate Luke's portrait of devout Jewish families and his respect for the temple and Torah, while noting tensions in the claim that Israel's hopes are fulfilled in Jesus. Christians read Luke's story as God keeping faith with Israel and through Israel bringing light to the nations.
37026: The Pharisee and the tax collector: legalism versus grace
37027: The parable is often preached as a contrast between the Jewish religion of works, represented by the Pharisee, and Christian grace, represented by the humble tax collector.
37028: Amy-Jill Levine and Kenneth Bailey note that both men pray in the temple, probably at the time of the daily atonement sacrifice, and that the Pharisee's fasting and tithing are admirable Jewish piety. The problem is contempt for others, which Luke names in the introduction. Levine even suggests the Greek may allow that the tax collector went home justified 'alongside' the Pharisee, a reading most scholars do not accept but which shows the parable's openness. The point is humility and mercy, aimed at every religious insider.
37029: Evangelical scholars such as Darrell Bock and Craig Blomberg agree the Pharisee should not be caricatured but stress that the parable does teach justification as God's merciful verdict on one who relies on mercy rather than his own record, a theme Paul develops. Both sides agree the story warns believers against the Pharisee's attitude, not against Judaism.
37030: Using the Pharisee as a symbol of Judaism turns a warning to the reader into a weapon against others, which is exactly the attitude the parable condemns.
37031: The Good Samaritan is simply 'be nice to strangers'
37032: The parable is often reduced to a lesson in helping people in need, with the priest and Levite as heartless religious types who would not risk ritual impurity.
37033: Levine argues the purity excuse does not fit: the priest is going down from Jerusalem, and Jewish law gave saving life priority. The shock is that the hero is a Samaritan, a hated enemy. The lawyer asked 'who is my neighbour?'; Jesus asks him to imagine being rescued by his enemy and to love like that, fulfilling Leviticus 19:18 and 19:34.
37034: Traditional commentators (for example Darrell Bock) largely agree about the enemy theme and the command of neighbour-love; many still see purity concerns as part of the backdrop, and some read the Samaritan as a picture of Christ's mercy. The disagreement is about details, not the call to costly mercy across hostile lines.
37035: Reading Judaism as the obstacle hides the parable's real demand: to love people from groups we fear or despise.
37036: Luke assured a mixed, mostly Gentile church that its faith rested on solid history and on Israel's own promises, and it modelled a community where rich and poor, Jew and Gentile, men and women shared one table.
37037: Luke challenges how readers handle money, status and hospitality, calls for prayer and openness to the Spirit, and invites them to see God's faithfulness to Israel as the root of their own hope.
37038: A reflective Gospel showing Jesus as the eternal Word who has 'tabernacled' among Israel, fulfilling its feasts and temple, so that readers may trust him and have life.
37039: The Beloved Disciple (traditionally John son of Zebedee)
37040: The Gospel rests on the witness of 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', who leaned on Jesus at the last supper and stood at the cross. He seems to have known Jerusalem and the temple intimately. The final chapter says others ('we know that his testimony is true') put the work into its final form.
37041: Irenaeus (c. 180) says John, the Lord's disciple, published the Gospel in Ephesus. Papias mentions both the apostle John and a 'John the Elder', so some scholars, including Richard Bauckham and Martin Hengel, think the Beloved Disciple was the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple not among the Twelve. Raymond Brown and others reconstructed a 'Johannine community' that shaped the Gospel in stages. Conservative scholars such as D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg defend the son of Zebedee.
37042: Revelation (traditionally; most scholars think a different John)
37043: Ephesus (traditional); some propose Syria or Palestine
37044: Ephesus is the unanimous early tradition. Its Jewish community and its temple of Artemis and imperial temple provide a plausible setting, but internal evidence does not settle the place.
37045: Believers, Jewish and Gentile, some of whom had been pushed out of synagogue fellowship, and possibly enquirers
37047: After 70, debate between Jesus-believing Jews and other Jews about Jesus' identity had become bitter, and the Gospel speaks of confessors being 'put out of the synagogue'. Whether this reflects one local community's experience or a broader process is debated.
37048: About three years, measured by at least three Passovers, from John the Baptist's testimony to the resurrection appearances.
37049: Pontius Pilate becomes prefect of Judea (to 36).
37051: Temple destroyed; John presents Jesus' body as the true temple.
37052: Approximate date often proposed for John's final form.
37053: Death of Domitian; Nerva becomes emperor.
37054:
John's Gospel is different from the other three. There are few parables and no exorcisms; instead there are seven 'signs', long conversations and speeches, and the great 'I am' sayings. Much of the action happens in Jerusalem at the Jewish feasts: Passover, Tabernacles and Dedication (Hanukkah). Jesus' public ministry spans at least three Passovers, which is where the traditional three-year ministry comes from.

Most scholars date the final form to the 90s, though a minority, following J. A. T. Robinson, argues for before 70, noting that John describes the pool of Bethesda as still standing. Since the 1960s J. Louis Martyn and Raymond Brown read John on 'two levels': the story of Jesus, and the story of a later community expelled from synagogues. That model has been criticised in recent decades, for example by Richard Bauckham, who argues the Gospels were written for a wide Christian readership, and by scholars who doubt there was any formal expulsion policy, so 'Johannine community' reconstructions should be held lightly.

Archaeology has strengthened John's local knowledge: the pool of Bethesda with five porticoes and the pool of Siloam have been excavated, and stone water jars like those at Cana fit a Jewish concern with purity. John's language of light and darkness, truth and lies, once thought Greek, has close parallels in the Dead Sea Scrolls, a Jewish setting.
37056: John organises much of Jesus' work around feasts. At Passover he feeds a crowd and speaks of bread from heaven; at Tabernacles, with its water-pouring and great lamps, he offers living water and calls himself light of the world; at Hanukkah, the feast of the temple's rededication, he speaks of being consecrated by the Father.
37057: The Word 'tabernacled' among us, and Jesus speaks of the temple of his body. For people who lost the temple in 70, this said God's presence had not abandoned them.
37059: Six stone water jars at Cana were for Jewish purification; stone did not contract impurity. Jesus fills them with abundant wine, a sign of the messianic wedding feast.
37060: The rare word aposynagogos describes being excluded from synagogue fellowship, a deep loss of family, community and identity in a collectivist culture. Older scholarship linked this to a curse on heretics in Jewish prayer, a link now widely doubted.
37062: 'The Jews' (or 'Judeans') in John usually means Jerusalem authorities opposing Jesus, sometimes Judeans in contrast to Galileans, and sometimes ordinary Jewish crowds, many of whom believe. Jesus and every disciple in the story are themselves Jews.
37063:
John is soaked in Israel's Scriptures and worship. It begins with 'In the beginning', retelling Genesis 1, and uses Jewish wisdom tradition, where Wisdom was with God at creation and came to dwell in Israel, to describe Jesus as the Word. Jesus is the Passover lamb, the manna from heaven, the bronze serpent lifted up, the true vine (Israel's own image in Isaiah and the Psalms), the good shepherd promised in Ezekiel 34, and the one who speaks the divine 'I am'. Salvation, Jesus tells a Samaritan woman, 'is from the Jews'.

The Gospel reflects a painful split within a Jewish family over who Jesus is. Its harsh language ('your father the devil') is the language of sectarian dispute among Jews, similar in tone to the Dead Sea Scrolls' attacks on other Jews, not a verdict on the Jewish people. Read inside Israel's covenant story, John's message is that the God who dwelt in the tabernacle and temple, who fed Israel in the wilderness and promised a shepherd-king, has come to his own in the flesh of a Jewish man, and that eternal life, the 'life of the age to come' hoped for in Daniel, begins now in knowing the Father through him.
37065: The eternal Word, agent of creation, tabernacles among Israel and reveals the Father's glory.
37067: Water to wine, the temple scene, Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman show new life replacing the old forms.
37069: At Sabbath, Passover, Tabernacles and Hanukkah Jesus reveals himself as bread, water, light and shepherd.
37071: The raising of Lazarus leads directly to the decision to kill Jesus.
37073: Jesus washes feet, gives the love command, promises the Spirit and prays for his followers' unity.
37075: Arrest, trial before Pilate and crucifixion at Passover are presented as Jesus' royal glorification.
37077: The risen Jesus meets Mary, Thomas and Peter; the stated purpose is that readers believe and have life.
37101: God's self-expression; echoes God speaking creation into being and Jewish Wisdom dwelling with Israel.
37103: To trust and commit oneself to someone; John uses the verb nearly a hundred times and never the noun.
37105: To stay, dwell, keep living in a relationship.
37106: Literally 'life of the age': the life of the age to come, begun now in knowing God.
37108: God's visible weighty presence, shown supremely in the cross.
37109: The prologue retells creation with Jesus as the Word through whom all things were made.
37110: Tabernacle, manna, Passover lamb and the divine name 'I am' all come from Exodus.
37111: The good shepherd and life-giving water flowing from the temple echo Ezekiel.
37112: Shares vocabulary (light, love, abide, truth) and confronts a later dispute about Jesus come in the flesh.
37113: John explicitly links Jesus' glory with Isaiah's temple vision and the rejected servant.
37114: John offers the New Testament's highest Christology: the Word was God, and Thomas confesses 'my Lord and my God'. Jewish readers have historically found John the most difficult Gospel because of its language about 'the Jews' and its claims about Jesus' divinity, though scholars such as Daniel Boyarin argue that ideas like a divine Word or second divine figure were themselves at home in Second Temple Judaism. Christians read John as the climax of Israel's hope that God would dwell with his people.
37115: 'The Jews' in John means the Jewish people as enemies of Jesus
37116: Reading English translations, many assume John portrays 'the Jews' as a whole as Jesus' opponents, and some have taken John 8:44 as a statement about Jewish people in general.
37117: Adele Reinhartz, Raymond Brown and the Jewish Annotated New Testament note that Ioudaioi often refers to Judean religious authorities, and that the Gospel's sharp polemic reflects an intra-Jewish dispute. Jesus, his mother, his disciples and the Beloved Disciple are all Jews, many 'Jews' believe in him, and Jesus says 'salvation is from the Jews'. Some translators render it 'Judeans' or 'Jewish leaders' in context; Reinhartz cautions that this can also hide the Gospel's real hostility, which readers should face honestly.
37118: Evangelical scholars such as D. A. Carson and Craig Keener agree John is not antisemitic in intent and that the term must be read in context, while noting that John does present a real conflict over Jesus' identity that cannot be softened away. Keener stresses the shared Jewish setting. There is no serious scholarly support today for using the text against Jewish people.
37119: John was used in sermons that fed medieval and modern antisemitism. Reading it in context honours both the Gospel's claims and Jesus' own people.
37120: Eternal life means only living forever in heaven after death
37121: John 3:16 is often heard as a promise that believers will not go to hell but will live forever in heaven when they die.
37122: In Jewish thought 'the age to come' was the time of God's renewal of creation and resurrection. John's 'life of the age' begins now: 'this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God'. It is relational knowing, not just endless duration, and it points to bodily resurrection on the last day. Scholars from Raymond Brown to N. T. Wright and Craig Keener stress this present and future shape.
37123: Evangelical scholars fully agree that eternal life is present and relational, and point out that John also clearly speaks of perishing and judgment and of future resurrection, so the popular reading is incomplete rather than wrong.
37124: Seeing eternal life as a present relationship with God turns faith from a ticket into a life of abiding and love.
37125: For believers who had lost the temple and possibly their synagogue community, John said God's dwelling was now found in Jesus and in a community of love, and that their trust in him was the fulfilment of Israel's worship.
37126: John invites readers to trust and abide in Jesus personally, to love one another visibly, and to read the Gospel's polemic with care, never turning it against Jewish neighbours.
37127: The story of how the risen Jesus, by his Spirit, restored a renewed Israel in Jerusalem and drew the nations in, carrying the hope of Israel from Jerusalem to Rome.
37128: Traditionally Luke, author of the Third Gospel
37129: A cultured writer, comfortable in Greek historiography and the Greek Old Testament, who knew the eastern Mediterranean well. The 'we' passages place him with Paul on parts of his journeys, including the voyage to Rome.
